screens.title: Setting Up Your Game Development Environment
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll set up the tools you need to prototype and build games with Unity. We'll walk through installing Unity Hub, adding a stable Editor version, and creating a new 3D project so you can start building right away. You'll also meet the core Editor windows — Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector — and learn the simple actions that let you place and move objects in the world. This matters because a reliable environment frees you to iterate quickly; missing build support or the wrong Editor version can block export later. For example, selecting Android or iOS build support when you install saves time if you later target mobile. I'll show a minimal hands-on activity: creating a plane and a sphere, setting the sphere's Y position so it sits on the plane, and using the move tool to drag it. By the end you'll have your first Unity project ready and a small scene to practice with. Think about one platform you might publish to and make sure you plan which build modules you need.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your first hands-on steps with Unity. You will first learn to download and install Unity Hub and use it to add a recommended Editor version. Installing through the Hub ensures you can manage multiple Editor versions and add platform build support. Next, you'll create a new Unity project from a 3D template and set a clear project name and location, which matters for project organization and version control later. You'll also learn to identify and use the primary Editor windows: Scene for building the world, Game for player view, Hierarchy for the scene's object list, Project as the asset browser, and Inspector for editing properties. Finally, you'll practice simple Editor actions like creating a 3D object, changing its Transform values, and using the Move tool. Each skill reduces friction when you prototype: knowing where assets live, how to move objects, and which build modules to install prevents common setup errors. As you work, notice the difference between Scene and Game views and practice the move, rotate, and scale tools to build comfort.

screens.title: Install Unity Hub — your central command center
screens.narratorSegment: Installing Unity Hub is the first practical step. Unity Hub manages Editor installations and projects so you don't install Editors manually. Start by visiting the download page and choosing the Hub installer. Run the installer and follow the prompts; accept the license and choose a comfortable install location. After installation open Hub and sign in with a Unity ID; if you don't have one, create it during sign-in. This Unity ID links your license and access to services. Once signed in, explore the Hub's main panes: Projects, Installs, and Learn. The Installs tab is where you'll add Editor versions; the Projects tab lists your projects and provides quick access to create or open them. A common misconception is that you should download an Editor directly from a website — instead, Hub centralizes versions and simplifies adding modules later. As a concrete example, imagine you plan to publish to mobile: in the Installs tab you can choose an LTS Editor and include mobile build support modules up front. Takeaway: Hub keeps versions organized and reduces future friction when adding or removing Editors.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Install Unity Hub
Install Unity Hub — your central command center
Download, run the installer, sign in, and use Hub to manage Editors and projects
Step-by-step
1. Download Unity Hub installer
2. Run installer and follow prompts
3. Open Hub and sign in or create a Unity ID
4. Explore Projects and Installs tabs
Key Takeaway

Unity Hub centralizes versions and projects; install Hub first to avoid scattered Editors.

Why this matters

Hub simplifies adding and removing Editor versions and installing platform modules. It helps you keep stable LTS versions for production work while testing newer releases separately.

Concrete example
Choose an LTS release in Installs and add Android build support now rather than later; it prevents export failures when you first try to build an APK.
Common mistake: Installing multiple Editors manually instead of through Hub, which complicates version management.

screens.title: Unity Hub vs Unity Editor
screens.narratorSegment: The terms 'Unity Hub' and 'Unity Editor' are often used together but they are different. Unity Hub is a desktop application for managing Editor versions, projects, and learning resources. The Unity Editor is the actual application that opens a project and provides the Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector windows where you build and configure your game. A useful way to think about it: Hub is your version manager and project launcher, while the Editor is the workspace where development happens. A common misconception is that the Hub is optional; technically you can install an Editor directly, but that loses the convenience of centralized updates and module management. A concrete example: you might keep an LTS Editor for stable development and a newer release for experimenting. Hub lets you install both without conflict and add modules per Editor, such as Android build support. Takeaway: treat Hub as your organizer and the Editor as your primary tool. When you plan projects, decide which Editor version you will use and install required platform modules up front to avoid later build errors. Unity Hub vs Unity Editor means hub organizes installations and projects; editor is where you build scenes and scripts.. In practical terms, understand the role of each tool and why both are needed. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Hub vs Editor
Unity Hub vs Unity Editor
Roles explained so you know what to install and why
Unity Hub
  • Manages multiple Editor versions and projects.
  • Makes it easy to add modules per Editor (platform build support).
  • Offers a centralized Projects list and learning resources.
Concrete example
Install an LTS Editor and an experimental Editor side-by-side via Hub without version conflict.
Unity Editor
  • The workspace for building scenes and editing GameObjects.
  • Contains Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector windows.
  • Where you attach components and script behaviors to objects.
Takeaway
Hub organizes; the Editor is where your work happens. Use Hub to control installs, Editor to build.

screens.title: Install the Unity Editor and select modules
screens.narratorSegment: When you add a Unity Editor through Hub, pick the recommended Long Term Support (LTS) release unless you have a specific reason to test a newer build. LTS releases receive stability and bug fixes and are recommended for new projects. Click 'Install Editor' in Hub's Installs tab, select the desired version, and choose the modules you need. Modules include platform build support like Android and iOS, and optional items such as documentation. A practical tip: select build support for the platforms you expect to target now. The most common mistake is skimming module choices and skipping mobile or desktop build support because you think you can add them later; adding them initially saves re-downloading components. For example, if you plan to prototype on Android, select Android Build Support. If you later add modules, Hub can attach them to that Editor but the initial install streamlines your first build attempts. Takeaway: install an LTS Editor with the right modules to avoid platform export errors during prototyping. Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Install Editor & Modules
Install the Unity Editor and select modules
Choose LTS, pick platform support, and avoid skipping modules you need
Recommended flow
  1. Open Installs tab and click Install Editor.
  2. Select the LTS version recommended by Hub.
  3. Choose modules: Documentation, Android/iOS Build Support, Windows/Mac if needed.
  4. Start installation and wait patiently while modules download.
Concrete example
Select Android Build Support during install if you intend to test on an Android device; this prevents build-time failures when exporting an APK.
Common mistake

Skipping build support modules and later discovering you cannot export to your target platform. Hub can add modules later, but initial selection is faster.

Key Takeaway

Choose an LTS Editor and add platform modules up front to reduce friction when building for your target device.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Create New Project
Create a new 3D project in Unity Hub
Select the 3D Core template and pick clear names and a location
Quick steps
  1. Open Projects tab and click New Project.
  2. Select 3D Core template for a minimal setup.
  3. Name the project and choose a save location.
  4. Click Create and wait while the Editor opens and imports assets.
Concrete example

Start projects with a minimal template and clear naming to stay organized and efficient.

screens.title: Scene View — your level editor
screens.narratorSegment: Scene View is the interactive workspace where you compose the game world. It is the place you place, move, rotate, and scale objects to build levels and test layouts. Navigation controls use common mouse patterns: right-click and drag to look around, scroll wheel to zoom, and middle-click to pan. You can also select an object and press 'F' to frame it, which centers the camera on that object. Scene View differs from Game View: Scene is the editor's construction canvas, while Game View shows what the player will see when the game runs. A common misconception is that Scene View output equals final rendering; the Game View is the player's perspective and respects the main camera's settings. A concrete example: after adding a Plane and a Sphere, use right-click to orbit around the Sphere and press 'F' to recenter the view. Practicing navigation empowers you to place objects precisely and speeds iteration. Takeaway: master Scene navigation early to move from idea to playable layout quickly. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Scene View
Scene View — your level editor
Navigate and arrange objects while composing your scene
Core interactions
  • Right-click + drag to look around.
  • Scroll wheel to zoom in and out.
  • Middle-click and drag to pan.
  • Select object and press 'F' to frame it.
Concrete example
After adding a Sphere, use right-click to orbit and press 'F' to center the view on it for precise placement.
Scene vs Game

Scene View is for editing; Game View renders the player's camera output. Changes in Scene affect Game when you run the scene but visual differences can occur due to camera settings and post-processing.

Key Takeaway

Learn navigation shortcuts and framing so you can quickly position objects and iterate on level design.

screens.title: Game View and the Main Camera
screens.narratorSegment: Game View is the player's rendered perspective and is driven by the scene's Main Camera. While Scene View gives you freedom to orbit and pan, Game View shows exactly what your camera sees, including viewport size, aspect ratio, and camera settings. Adjusting the Main Camera's transform, field of view, or clear flags will change the Game View output. A common misconception is to assume the Scene perspective equals the player's view; it does not. For example, you can place lights and objects in Scene that look different when seen through the camera because of framing and projection. A concrete walkthrough: place a cube at origin, create a camera slightly offset back, then open Game View and observe how moving the camera left or right changes what the player sees. Use Game View to test framing, UI placement, and aspect ratios for target devices. Takeaway: always test visuals in Game View to verify player-facing composition and camera settings. Game View and the Main Camera means use game view to verify what the player sees; adjust the main camera for framing and device aspect ratios.. In practical terms, how the game view differs from scene and why the camera matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Game View & Camera
Game View and the Main Camera
Understand camera-driven rendering and verify player perspective
What Game View shows
  • The player's rendered perspective from the Main Camera.
  • Viewport resolution and aspect ratio for testing UI and framing.
  • How camera settings like field of view affect composition.
Concrete example
Place a cube at the origin and move the Main Camera back; Game View will show the cube centered while Scene may be at a different angle.
Practical tip

Use Game View to test aspect ratios for target devices and make small camera adjustments for better player framing before adding polish.

Key Takeaway

Game View reflects the camera's output—use it to validate what players actually experience.

screens.title: Hierarchy vs Project Window
screens.narratorSegment: Hierarchy and Project are two different but complementary windows. The Hierarchy lists GameObjects present in the currently open Scene — it represents the active scene graph. The Project window is your asset browser: it stores all project files such as scripts, models, textures, audio, and scenes, regardless of whether they are currently in the scene. A common confusion for beginners is dragging an asset into Hierarchy and expecting it to disappear from Project — dragging creates an instance in the Scene while leaving the original asset in the Project window. For example, if you drag a model from Project into the Scene, the model appears in Hierarchy as a GameObject; the file still exists in Project. Use Hierarchy to manage scene composition and parent-child relationships, using nesting when grouping objects. Use Project to organize and locate assets and to create prefabs you can reuse. Takeaway: Project is your library; Hierarchy is what’s placed into the active scene. Understanding this separation helps you keep assets reusable and scenes tidy. In practical terms, scene objects versus project assets — where each belongs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A common confusion for beginners is dragging an asset into Hierarchy and expecting it to disappear from Project — dragging creates an instance in the Scene while leaving the original asset in the Project window. For example, if you drag a model from Project into the Scene, the model appears in Hierarchy as a GameObject; the file still exists in Project. Use Hierarchy to manage scene composition and parent-child relationships, using nesting when grouping objects. Use Project to organize and locate assets and to create prefabs you can reuse. Takeaway: Project is your library; Hierarchy is what’s placed into the active scene. Understanding this separation helps you keep assets reusable and scenes tidy. Hierarchy vs Project Window means project holds source assets; hierarchy lists instances in the current scene. drag from project to scene to instantiate.. In practical terms, scene objects versus project assets — where each belongs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Hierarchy & Project
Hierarchy vs Project Window
Understand scene instances and project assets and how they interact
Hierarchy (Scene instances)
  • Shows GameObjects currently placed in the active scene.
  • Supports parent-child nesting for grouping and transforms inheritance.
  • Use it to organize and select scene instances for editing.
Project (Asset library)

  • Drag assets from Project into the Scene or Hierarchy to instantiate them.

Drag a 3D model from Project into the Scene. It appears in Hierarchy as an instance; the source file remains in Project.

screens.title: Inspector Window and Components
screens.narratorSegment: The Inspector displays properties and components for the currently selected GameObject or asset. Components are modular pieces of functionality you attach to GameObjects to give them behavior or appearance, such as Transform, Mesh Renderer, Colliders, or custom scripts. Selecting a Cube shows its Transform with Position, Rotation, and Scale fields in the Inspector. You can edit numeric values directly or use the Editor manipulation tools. A common misconception is that changing a value in Scene is always temporary; changes in the Inspector persist to the scene unless you undo them. For example, selecting a Sphere and setting its Position Y to 0.5 in the Inspector places it above a Plane so it sits on the surface. You can also add or remove components in the Inspector to alter behavior. Takeaway: use the Inspector to make precise adjustments and to add components that change a GameObject’s function, rather than trying to edit behaviors only through Scene manipulation. Inspector Window and Components means inspector edits components which define what a gameobject is and how it behaves; transform is the core component for spatial positioning.. screens.title: Create your first 3D objects — Plane and Sphere
screens.narratorSegment: Let's create a simple scene to practice. In the Hierarchy window right-click, navigate to '3D Object', and select 'Plane' to create ground. Next, right-click again and choose '3D Object' → 'Sphere' to add a player placeholder. With the Sphere selected, look at the Inspector and find the Transform component. Change Position Y to 0.5 so the Sphere sits on top of the Plane rather than intersecting it. This small numeric edit ensures accurate placement, which is especially helpful when objects must align or when physics is involved. A common beginner mistake is leaving objects with overlapping transforms which leads to clipping and physics instability. Use the Move tool (press 'W') to drag the Sphere around and practice aligning it with the plane. A concrete practice: after placing the Sphere, press 'F' to frame it in Scene View and then press 'W' to use the Move tool and drag it along axes. Module 2 › Chapter 1.3 › Create Plane & Sphere
Create your first 3D objects — Plane and Sphere
Add primitives to prototype physics, placement, and scale
Step-by-step
  1. In Hierarchy: Right-click → 3D Object → Plane.
  2. Right-click → 3D Object → Sphere.

Concrete example

Common mistake

Placing objects at overlapping positions without correcting transforms causes clipping or unintended physics collisions. Use numeric edits and framing to avoid this.

Key Takeaway

Start with primitives to quickly prototype layout and physics behavior before bringing in complex assets.

screens.title: Editor manipulation tools: Move, Rotate, Scale (W, E, R)
screens.narratorSegment: Unity provides three primary manipulation tools to position and orient objects: Move, Rotate, and Scale. You can access them with the W, E, and R keys respectively. The Move tool shows axis handles that let you drag an object along X, Y, or Z; use constrained axis dragging for precise placement. The Rotate tool uses circular handles to change orientation, and Scale provides handles to change size either uniformly or per axis. A subtle point is that the numeric Transform fields in the Inspector and the visual handles in Scene are both authoritative; use whichever is faster. For example, to place a cube precisely at X = 1.5, enter the numeric value in the Inspector. To rotate an object for visual polish, use the Rotate tool and fine-tune angles in Inspector. A common misconception is that the tools are modal and lose state; they are persistent until you switch, so remember which tool you're using. Takeaway: practice toggling W, E, and R and combine numeric edits with visual handles for both quick layout and precise adjustments. In practical terms, use tools and shortcuts to shape your scene quickly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.narratorSegment: Now put the setup knowledge into practice with a short activity. Open Unity Hub, create a 3D project named 'MyFirstScene', and open it in the Editor. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll set up the tools you need to prototype and build games with Unity. We'll walk through installing Unity Hub, adding a stable Editor version, and creating a new 3D project so you can start building right away. You'll also meet the core Editor windows — Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector — and learn the simple actions that let you place and move objects in the world. This matters because a reliable environment frees you to iterate quickly; missing build support or the wrong Editor version can block export later. For example, selecting Android or iOS build support when you install saves time if you later target mobile. I'll show a minimal hands-on activity: creating a plane and a sphere, setting the sphere's Y position so it sits on the plane, and using the move tool to drag it. By the end you'll have your first Unity project ready and a small scene to practice with. Think about one platform you might publish to and make sure you plan which build modules you need.

These objectives focus your first hands-on steps with Unity. You will first learn to download and install Unity Hub and use it to add a recommended Editor version. Installing through the Hub ensures you can manage multiple Editor versions and add platform build support. Next, you'll create a new Unity project from a 3D template and set a clear project name and location, which matters for project organization and version control later. You'll also learn to identify and use the primary Editor windows: Scene for building the world, Game for player view, Hierarchy for the scene's object list, Project as the asset browser, and Inspector for editing properties. Finally, you'll practice simple Editor actions like creating a 3D object, changing its Transform values, and using the Move tool. Each skill reduces friction when you prototype: knowing where assets live, how to move objects, and which build modules to install prevents common setup errors. As you work, notice the difference between Scene and Game views and practice the move, rotate, and scale tools to build comfort.

These same objectives framed as hands-on outcomes will guide your first session. First, get Unity Hub installed and use it to install an LTS Unity Editor with the build modules you'll need. Picking the correct modules at install time, like Android or iOS support when you intend to target mobile, will prevent export errors later. Second, create a new 3D project with a clear name and location so you can find and version it later. Third, become fluent with the Editor windows: Scene for composing levels, Game for the player's rendered view, Hierarchy for the scene object tree, Project as your asset library, and Inspector to edit selected objects. Finally, complete the activity: add a Plane for ground, add a Sphere as a player placeholder, set its Y position to sit on the ground, and practice framing and moving it. These actions build a muscle memory that speeds future iteration and reduces friction when you prototype gameplay mechanics.

Installing Unity Hub is the first practical step. Unity Hub manages Editor installations and projects so you don't install Editors manually. Start by visiting the download page and choosing the Hub installer. Run the installer and follow the prompts; accept the license and choose a comfortable install location. After installation open Hub and sign in with a Unity ID; if you don't have one, create it during sign-in. This Unity ID links your license and access to services. Once signed in, explore the Hub's main panes: Projects, Installs, and Learn. The Installs tab is where you'll add Editor versions; the Projects tab lists your projects and provides quick access to create or open them. A common misconception is that you should download an Editor directly from a website — instead, Hub centralizes versions and simplifies adding modules later. As a concrete example, imagine you plan to publish to mobile: in the Installs tab you can choose an LTS Editor and include mobile build support modules up front. Takeaway: Hub keeps versions organized and reduces future friction when adding or removing Editors.

The terms 'Unity Hub' and 'Unity Editor' are often used together but they are different. Unity Hub is a desktop application for managing Editor versions, projects, and learning resources. The Unity Editor is the actual application that opens a project and provides the Scene, Game, Hierarchy, Project, and Inspector windows where you build and configure your game. A useful way to think about it: Hub is your version manager and project launcher, while the Editor is the workspace where development happens. A common misconception is that the Hub is optional; technically you can install an Editor directly, but that loses the convenience of centralized updates and module management. A concrete example: you might keep an LTS Editor for stable development and a newer release for experimenting. Hub lets you install both without conflict and add modules per Editor, such as Android build support. Takeaway: treat Hub as your organizer and the Editor as your primary tool. When you plan projects, decide which Editor version you will use and install required platform modules up front to avoid later build errors. Unity Hub vs Unity Editor means hub organizes installations and projects; editor is where you build scenes and scripts.. In practical terms, understand the role of each tool and why both are needed. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When you add a Unity Editor through Hub, pick the recommended Long Term Support (LTS) release unless you have a specific reason to test a newer build. LTS releases receive stability and bug fixes and are recommended for new projects. Click 'Install Editor' in Hub's Installs tab, select the desired version, and choose the modules you need. Modules include platform build support like Android and iOS, and optional items such as documentation. A practical tip: select build support for the platforms you expect to target now. The most common mistake is skimming module choices and skipping mobile or desktop build support because you think you can add them later; adding them initially saves re-downloading components. For example, if you plan to prototype on Android, select Android Build Support. If you later add modules, Hub can attach them to that Editor but the initial install streamlines your first build attempts. Takeaway: install an LTS Editor with the right modules to avoid platform export errors during prototyping. Install the Unity Editor and select modules means pick an lts editor and include necessary platform modules so builds succeed without reconfiguration later.. In practical terms, choose an lts editor and add platform build support. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Creating a new project is simple but important for good organization. In Unity Hub, open the Projects tab and click New Project. Choose the "3D Core" template for this course because it provides the minimal 3D setup without extra sample content. Give your project a meaningful name, for example 'MyFirstScene' or 'MyFirstUnityGame', and choose a clear file location on your disk. Good naming and placement help later when you use version control or share the project. After you click Create Project, Hub will open the Unity Editor and begin importing the initial packages. This can take a few moments. A typical misconception is to pick sample-heavy templates which clutter the Project window with unnecessary assets; prefer the minimal 3D template for learning and prototyping. Once the Editor opens, take a brief moment to let it finish importing. Then you'll see the default scene and the core windows ready for exploration. Takeaway: start projects with clear names and minimal templates to keep your workspace focused and lightweight. Create a new 3D project in Unity Hub means choose the '3d core' template, name your project, and store it where you can back it up and version it.. In practical terms, select the 3d core template, name your project, and create it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Scene View is the interactive workspace where you compose the game world. It is the place you place, move, rotate, and scale objects to build levels and test layouts. Navigation controls use common mouse patterns: right-click and drag to look around, scroll wheel to zoom, and middle-click to pan. You can also select an object and press 'F' to frame it, which centers the camera on that object. Scene View differs from Game View: Scene is the editor's construction canvas, while Game View shows what the player will see when the game runs. A common misconception is that Scene View output equals final rendering; the Game View is the player's perspective and respects the main camera's settings. A concrete example: after adding a Plane and a Sphere, use right-click to orbit around the Sphere and press 'F' to recenter the view. Practicing navigation empowers you to place objects precisely and speeds iteration. Takeaway: master Scene navigation early to move from idea to playable layout quickly. Scene View — your level editor means use right-click, scroll, and framing to navigate scene view and accurately place objects in your level.. In practical terms, what scene view is and how to interact with it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Game View is the player's rendered perspective and is driven by the scene's Main Camera. While Scene View gives you freedom to orbit and pan, Game View shows exactly what your camera sees, including viewport size, aspect ratio, and camera settings. Adjusting the Main Camera's transform, field of view, or clear flags will change the Game View output. A common misconception is to assume the Scene perspective equals the player's view; it does not. Hierarchy and Project are two different but complementary windows. The Hierarchy lists GameObjects present in the currently open Scene — it represents the active scene graph. The Project window is your asset browser: it stores all project files such as scripts, models, textures, audio, and scenes, regardless of whether they are currently in the scene. A common confusion for beginners is dragging an asset into Hierarchy and expecting it to disappear from Project — dragging creates an instance in the Scene while leaving the original asset in the Project window. For example, if you drag a model from Project into the Scene, the model appears in Hierarchy as a GameObject; the file still exists in Project. Use Hierarchy to manage scene composition and parent-child relationships, using nesting when grouping objects. Use Project to organize and locate assets and to create prefabs you can reuse. Takeaway: Project is your library; Hierarchy is what’s placed into the active scene. Understanding this separation helps you keep assets reusable and scenes tidy. The Inspector displays properties and components for the currently selected GameObject or asset. Components are modular pieces of functionality you attach to GameObjects to give them behavior or appearance, such as Transform, Mesh Renderer, Colliders, or custom scripts. Selecting a Cube shows its Transform with Position, Rotation, and Scale fields in the Inspector. You can edit numeric values directly or use the Editor manipulation tools. A common misconception is that changing a value in Scene is always temporary; changes in the Inspector persist to the scene unless you undo them. For example, selecting a Sphere and setting its Position Y to 0.5 in the Inspector places it above a Plane so it sits on the surface. You can also add or remove components in the Inspector to alter behavior. Takeaway: use the Inspector to make precise adjustments and to add components that change a GameObject’s function, rather than trying to edit behaviors only through Scene manipulation. Unity provides three primary manipulation tools to position and orient objects: Move, Rotate, and Scale. You can access them with the W, E, and R keys respectively. The Rotate tool uses circular handles to change orientation, and Scale provides handles to change size either uniformly or per axis. Let's summarize the essential concepts you need to continue. Unity is the engine and Editor you use to build games. Unity Hub is the manager you'll use to install different Editor versions and add platform modules. The Scene View is your construction canvas where you place, move, and edit objects; the Game View shows the player's rendered perspective from the Main Camera. The Inspector is the place to change a selected object's components and numeric Transform values. A quick example: you download Hub, install an LTS Editor with Android build support, create a 3D project, add a Plane and Sphere, set the Sphere's Y position to 0.5, and verify the camera framing in Game View. A common pitfall is skipping required modules during installation; plan your target platform before you finish installing the Editor. Keep practicing creating primitives, using W/E/R, and switching between Scene and Game — these habits speed up every prototype you build. Reflect: which window will you use most during prototyping and why?

A final set of concise definitions to keep at hand: the Hierarchy Window lists every GameObject in the active scene and reflects parent-child relationships. The Project Window is your asset browser containing models, scripts, textures, and scenes for the entire project. The Inspector Window displays and edits components and properties for the currently selected GameObject or asset. Remember that GameObjects are the items you place in scenes, and Components are the modular behaviors or properties you attach to those GameObjects, such as Transform, Mesh Renderer, or scripts. Concrete example: drag a model from Project into the Scene; it creates a GameObject visible in Hierarchy and its properties are editable in Inspector. A useful self-check is to name which window you'd use to locate an asset (Project) versus which you would use to change its position in the scene (Inspector or Move tool). Keep practicing these distinctions when you build scenes.
